blocks.content: If you have spent any time reading about software design, you have almost certainly run into the phrase design pattern. It gets mentioned in interviews, in code reviews, in books with names like a gang of authors on the cover.
For a beginner it can feel like a secret handshake. Experienced engineers throw around words like Factory, Observer, or Strategy as if everyone should already know what they mean.

This lesson is about pulling that curtain back. Before we look at any specific pattern, we want to understand why patterns exist at all, what problem they actually solve, and just as importantly, when they do not help.
Think of this as the "why" that should come before every "how". Once the why is solid, every individual pattern you learn later will make a lot more sense.
We will use one running example throughout this lesson, sending notifications through an app, to keep things concrete instead of abstract.
A design pattern is a proven, reusable solution to a problem that keeps showing up in software design, described in a form general enough to apply across many different codebases.
1. The Problem Design Patterns Actually Solve
blocks.text: 1. The Problem Design Patterns Actually Solve

blocks.content: A Familiar Situation
blocks.text: A Familiar Situation

blocks.content: Imagine you join a team and your first task is to add a new way to notify users, say push notifications, alongside the existing email and SMS notifications.
You open the codebase and find that email notifications are created one way in the billing module, a slightly different way in the signup module, and a third way in the reminders module.
Nobody planned it this way. Each engineer solved the same small problem independently, under time pressure, without knowing the others had already solved it too.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499303918-296399237.png
blocks.alt: One recurring problem branching into three modules that each solve it independently, ending in three different shapes with no shared name

blocks.content: What a Pattern Actually Is
blocks.text: What a Pattern Actually Is

blocks.content: A design pattern is not a library you import or a snippet you paste. It is a named, well understood shape for solving a recurring design problem.

The problem of "creating one of several related objects without hardcoding which one everywhere" is common enough that it has a name: the Factory pattern. Once you know the name, you also know the shape of the solution.

Notice that a pattern describes a shape, not exact code. The Factory pattern looks slightly different in JavaScript, Python, and Java, but the underlying idea, centralizing object creation, stays the same.
Patterns Are Not Tied to One Language
blocks.text: Patterns Are Not Tied to One Language

blocks.content: Because a pattern describes a relationship between roles rather than specific syntax, it survives across languages and frameworks. An engineer who learns the Observer pattern in one language recognizes it instantly in another.
This is part of why patterns are worth learning early. The investment carries forward into every language and every project you touch afterward.
2. Reinventing a Solution From Scratch Is Risky and Slow
blocks.text: 2. Reinventing a Solution From Scratch Is Risky and Slow

blocks.content: Starting From Zero Every Time
blocks.text: Starting From Zero Every Time

blocks.content: When a recurring problem has no agreed upon solution, every engineer who meets it starts from zero. Some of them will find a decent answer. Others will find a fragile one.
This is slower than it looks. Time gets spent debating an approach that has already been debated, refined, and battle tested by thousands of other engineers before you.
Worse, an untested, home grown solution usually has edge cases nobody thought about, because nobody stress tested it against real world usage the way an established pattern has been.
The Hidden Cost of Ad Hoc Code
blocks.text: The Hidden Cost of Ad Hoc Code

blocks.content: The cost of reinventing solutions rarely shows up immediately. It shows up months later, when three slightly different implementations of the same idea have to be maintained, debugged, and explained to new hires separately.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499306516-560075825.png
blocks.alt: One ad hoc solution fanning out into more bugs, more onboarding time, riskier code review, and riskier refactors

blocks.content: ["More bugs, because each ad hoc solution has its own untested edge cases","More onboarding time, because new engineers must learn several different approaches to the same problem","More code to review, because reviewers cannot rely on a shared, known shape","More risk during refactors, because there is no single place to change the approach"]
items: More bugs, because each ad hoc solution has its own untested edge cases
More onboarding time, because new engineers must learn several different approaches to the same problem
More code to review, because reviewers cannot rely on a shared, known shape
More risk during refactors, because there is no single place to change the approach

blocks.content: Speed Is Part of the Point Too
blocks.text: Speed Is Part of the Point Too

blocks.content: There is also a plain productivity argument here. An engineer who recognizes a problem as "this is a Factory situation" can jump almost straight to writing the solution, instead of spending an afternoon designing one from first principles.

That saved time compounds across a team. Multiply it by every engineer, every sprint, and every recurring problem, and the difference between a team that shares patterns and one that does not becomes very large.
3. A Problem Without a Pattern
blocks.text: 3. A Problem Without a Pattern

blocks.content: The Scenario
blocks.text: The Scenario

blocks.content: Let us make this concrete. Say our app needs to send email, SMS, and push notifications, and different parts of the codebase each need to send one.
Without any shared approach, each file that needs a notification writes its own logic for deciding which kind of notification object to build.

Notice what happened. The same "which notification do I build" logic got duplicated, and the second copy quietly dropped the push case. This is exactly the kind of drift that happens when there is no shared, named approach.
Multiply this by a dozen files and a few years of turnover, and you get a codebase where nobody is fully sure how many different ways notifications get created.
4. The Same Problem, Solved With a Pattern
blocks.text: 4. The Same Problem, Solved With a Pattern

blocks.content: Introducing a Factory
blocks.text: Introducing a Factory

blocks.content: The Factory pattern says, put the "which object do I build" decision in exactly one place, and let everyone else simply ask for what they need.
This is not a new idea we are inventing for this lesson. It is a well known, named shape that thousands of teams already use, which is exactly the point.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499307960-327623915.png
blocks.alt: Two caller modules both asking one NotificationFactory, which creates the Email, Sms, or Push notification classes

blocks.content: Now every caller asks the factory for a notification instead of rebuilding the decision logic itself. Adding a new channel, say a Slack notification, means touching one class instead of hunting down every copy.
This is a small example, but the same idea scales to much bigger systems. The pattern did not change what the code does. It changed where the decision lives and how many places need to agree on it.

blocks.title: Why this matters more than it looks
blocks.content: The bug in the ad hoc version, a silently dropped push case, is exactly the kind of mistake a shared, named pattern prevents, because there is only one place left where that mistake could happen.
What Changed, Exactly
blocks.text: What Changed, Exactly

blocks.content: It is worth being precise about what the pattern bought us here. The behavior of sending an email, an SMS, or a push notification did not change at all.
What changed is where the decision about which class to build lives. Before, that decision was copied into every file that needed a notification. After, it lives in exactly one class.
That single change is the entire value of the pattern in this example. Small on paper, but it is the difference between one bug fix and four scattered bug fixes.
5. Patterns Capture Hard Won Experience
blocks.text: 5. Patterns Capture Hard Won Experience

blocks.content: Standing on the Shoulders of Other Engineers
blocks.text: Standing on the Shoulders of Other Engineers

blocks.content: Design patterns did not come from a single afternoon of clever thinking. They were noticed after the fact, by engineers who kept seeing the same shape of solution appear again and again across unrelated projects.

When you use the Factory pattern, you are not just copying a syntax trick. You are inheriting decades of accumulated experience about what tends to go wrong when object creation is scattered, and what tends to go right when it is centralized.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499309297-106880758.png
blocks.alt: Three separate systems hitting the same problem, converging into one common shape that gets given a name, the Factory pattern

blocks.content: This is the real value underneath the jargon. A pattern is a distilled answer to "we tried this problem many times, and this shape kept working better than the alternatives".

blocks.title: Borrowed experience
blocks.text: A junior engineer who reaches for the Observer pattern to keep a UI in sync with changing data is quietly benefiting from every engineer before them who struggled with tangled, manual update logic and eventually converged on this same clean shape.

blocks.content: Patterns Were Discovered, Not Invented in a Vacuum
blocks.text: Patterns Were Discovered, Not Invented in a Vacuum

blocks.content: The engineers who first wrote about design patterns were mostly acting as observers. They looked at many separate, successful systems and noticed the same recurring shapes, then gave those shapes names.
That is an important detail. A pattern earning its name means it already survived contact with many real systems, not just one clever demo.
6. The Communication Benefit of a Shared Vocabulary
blocks.text: 6. The Communication Benefit of a Shared Vocabulary

blocks.content: Naming Cuts Through Explanation
blocks.text: Naming Cuts Through Explanation

blocks.content: Imagine explaining your notification design to a teammate without using the word "factory". You would need a paragraph describing how object creation is centralized, how new types get added, and why that matters.
Now imagine saying instead, "just use a factory here". One sentence, and if your teammate knows the pattern, they instantly picture the whole shape of the solution.
This is the second big reason patterns matter. They give engineers a shared vocabulary, the same way "binary search" lets you skip explaining an entire algorithm from scratch in a conversation.

{"headers":["Without a Shared Name","With a Shared Name"],"rows":[["\"Let us have one place that decides which notification class to instantiate based on a type string, and have every caller go through that instead of duplicating the check\"","\"Let us use a factory here\""],["\"Let us have a list of listeners that get called whenever this object changes, so the UI stays in sync automatically\"","\"Let us use the observer pattern here\""],["\"Let us make sure there is only ever one instance of this configuration object shared across the app\"","\"Let us make this a singleton\""]]}
The right hand column is not shorter because it skips detail. It is shorter because the detail already lives in a name both engineers understand.
This Shows Up in Code Review Too
blocks.text: This Shows Up in Code Review Too

blocks.content: A reviewer who sees a comment saying "applied the strategy pattern here so we can add new pricing rules later" understands the intent immediately, without needing the author to justify every class in the diff.

Without that shared name, the same reviewer might question why there are suddenly three extra classes for what looks like a simple calculation, and the author has to re-explain the reasoning from scratch.
7. Seeing the Difference
blocks.text: 7. Seeing the Difference

blocks.content: Scattered Solutions vs One Named Pattern
blocks.text: Scattered Solutions vs One Named Pattern

blocks.content: The diagram below shows the same idea we walked through in code. On one side, each module invents its own way to create a notification. On the other, every module asks one shared factory.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783494313295-472065756.png
blocks.alt: Scattered ad hoc notification creation across four modules compared to all four modules asking one shared notification factory

blocks.content: The red boxes on the left each drifted slightly from one another over time. The grey boxes on the right all depend on one blue box, so a fix or an addition only has to happen once.
8. Patterns Are Tools for Specific Situations, Not a Checklist
blocks.text: 8. Patterns Are Tools for Specific Situations, Not a Checklist

blocks.content: The Overuse Trap
blocks.text: The Overuse Trap

blocks.content: Here is the honest part that often gets skipped. Design patterns are not a checklist you should try to apply to every piece of code you write.
A junior engineer who has just learned about the Factory pattern will sometimes reach for it even when a plain function returning an object would have been perfectly fine.
Forcing a pattern onto a problem that does not need it adds indirection, extra classes, and extra reading for whoever comes after you, without buying anything in return.
A Simple Filter
blocks.text: A Simple Filter

blocks.content: Before reaching for a named pattern, it is worth asking whether the problem you are looking at is actually the recurring problem that pattern was built for, or whether you are just excited to use something you recently learned.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499310732-747813936.png
blocks.alt: A decision flow asking whether a problem genuinely recurs, branching to reaching for a named pattern or writing plain simple code

blocks.content: {"pros":["Gives you a proven, tested shape instead of an untested guess","Creates a shared vocabulary so teammates understand your intent instantly","Makes future changes easier when the underlying problem genuinely recurs","Reduces subtle bugs caused by duplicated, drifting ad hoc logic"],"cons":["Adds indirection and extra files when the underlying problem is trivial","Can signal cleverness for its own sake rather than clarity","Makes code harder to follow for readers unfamiliar with that particular pattern","Becomes a crutch if used to avoid thinking about the actual problem"]}

blocks.title: A grounded rule of thumb
blocks.content: Reach for a pattern when you notice the same design problem recurring, or when you can already tell a simple version will need to grow. Do not reach for one just because a diagram or a book mentioned it.
A Word on Over Engineering
blocks.text: A Word on Over Engineering

blocks.content: There is a well known joke in software circles about an engineer asked to print "hello world" who instead builds a factory of factories, an abstract greeting strategy, and a configurable message provider.
It is a joke because everyone recognizes the pattern of the joke. Somewhere, a simple two line function turned into a small architecture, and nobody involved is better off for it.
The lesson is not that patterns are bad. The lesson is that a pattern applied to a problem too small for it adds cost without adding value, which is the opposite of what a pattern is supposed to do.
9. Questions to Ask Before Reaching for a Pattern
blocks.text: 9. Questions to Ask Before Reaching for a Pattern

blocks.content: A Short Checklist
blocks.text: A Short Checklist

blocks.content: These questions are not a formula, but they are a useful gut check before adding a named pattern to a piece of code.

["Have I seen this exact shape of problem before, in this codebase or another one","Would a plain function or a plain object solve this just as clearly, with less ceremony","Will this part of the system likely need new variants added later","Would naming this pattern actually help a teammate understand my intent faster","Am I choosing this pattern because it fits, or because I want to practice using it"]
items: Have I seen this exact shape of problem before, in this codebase or another one
Would a plain function or a plain object solve this just as clearly, with less ceremony
Will this part of the system likely need new variants added later
Would naming this pattern actually help a teammate understand my intent faster
Am I choosing this pattern because it fits, or because I want to practice using it

blocks.content: If most of the honest answers point toward "yes, this genuinely recurs and naming it would help", a pattern is probably earning its place. If not, plain code is usually the better choice.
It Is Fine to Start Simple
blocks.text: It Is Fine to Start Simple

blocks.content: A common, healthy path is to write the plain version first, and only introduce a named pattern once the plain version actually starts showing the strain, extra branches, duplicated logic, or new variants piling up.

Patterns applied at that point tend to fit naturally, because the code is telling you what shape it wants. Patterns applied too early tend to feel forced, because you are guessing at a shape the problem has not asked for yet.
10. Wrapping Up
blocks.text: 10. Wrapping Up

blocks.content: Design patterns exist because the same handful of design problems show up over and over across unrelated codebases, and reinventing an answer each time is slower and riskier than reusing one that has already been proven.
They also give engineers a shared vocabulary. Saying "use a factory" replaces a paragraph of explanation with a single, precise word.

But a pattern is a tool for a specific situation, not a badge to collect or a checklist to complete. The engineers who use patterns well are the ones who can also recognize when the simplest possible code is the right answer.

As you learn individual patterns in the lessons that follow, keep coming back to this question: what recurring problem is this pattern actually solving, and is that the problem in front of me right now.

Hold onto the notification example from earlier. Every pattern you learn next is solving some version of the same underlying story, one recurring problem, one proven shape, and one name that lets you talk about it quickly with anyone else who already knows it.
